The Cinque Ports. Five fortified English coastal towns—Hastings, New Romney, Hythe, Dover, and Sandwich—formed a historic maritime confederation established in the medieval period to organize naval defense and commerce along the southeastern English coast. Granted royal charters and privileges in exchange for maintaining ships and military readiness, the Cinque Ports formed an early coordinated system of maritime administration and became some of medieval England's wealthiest and most influential towns.

These five ports controlled vital shipping lanes across the English Channel and served as England's primary naval bulwark against French and Continental threats. Their merchants enjoyed monopolies on wine imports and other goods, accumulating vast wealth and political power in medieval England. The confederation had its own court, called the Court of Brotherhood and Guestling, to adjudicate disputes between members. They were first formally recognized by royal charter in the twelfth century, with privileges expanded through the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Two additional ports, Winchelsea and Rye, were later added as confederate members, expanding the original five into a larger maritime network.

Their importance declined after the Tudor period as naval power became centered on permanent royal warships rather than merchant vessels, and control of the English Channel shifted from merchant confederations to centralized royal authority.
